title: Places and journeys
job: A trip told in full, with directions inside it
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: Rōmam eō (to a city, no preposition)
Rōmā veniō (from a city, no preposition)

rules.text: CITY NAMES TAKE NO PREPOSITION, AND NEITHER DOES home. Rōmam eō 'I go to Rome', Rōmā veniō 'I come from Rome' — the ending carries the relation, exactly as L2-M4's domum and domō do. This module generalises that pattern from home to city names, and NOTHING ELSE IN THE LANGUAGE DOES IT: every other noun needs ad, ā or in. Thirty-seven modules have taught ad scholam, so ad Rōmam is the reflex — and it is wrong.

THE LOCATIVE IS A WHOLE CASE SURVIVING FOR A HANDFUL OF WORDS, and L2-M4 named domī as deferred TWENTY-NINE MODULES AGO. Rōmae is 'at Rome' and domī is 'at home', and Latin lost this case everywhere else. So it is not a rule to generalise but a list to learn: city names, domus, and two or three more. L3-M7 wanted domī for melius est … manēre and wrote domum īre instead; M8 wrote Rōmae before this module could explain it. Both borrowings are now paid off, and the set is complete — domum to, domō from, domī at.

A CLOSED LIST HAS TO BE FENCED ON BOTH SIDES, so this module writes TWO mistake plates rather than one. ad Rōmam eō is the error thirty-seven modules of ad scholam produce; scholam eō is the error over-generalising this module produces. Both are in S05, three words apart, because the only honest way to teach a rule that applies to a handful of words is to show what happens on each side of it. in Rōmā and ā Rōmā are the third and fourth wrong prepositions, and each is correct somewhere else.

Rōmae IS A LOCATIVE AND ALSO A GENITIVE, and nothing parts them. The locative of a first-declension city name is identical to its genitive singular — which is the same collision L2-M2 named for magistrī and L3-M8 for librī: no mark, no gate, and the sentence decides. This course writes only the locative reading and names the other here.

A JOURNEY IN LATIN HAS FAR FEWER PREPOSITIONS THAN ONE IN ENGLISH. Rōmā rēctā domum vēnī has three relations in it — from, by-a-straight-route, to — and not one preposition, because each is an ending. L2-M4's ad dextram keeps its ad, because a direction is not a place. Counting prepositions is the quickest way to see how much of this language lives in its endings.

A TRIP TOLD IN FULL USES THE WHOLE LEVEL: M6's cum with a subjunctive, M8's imperfect for what went on and the perfect for what happened once, L2-M10's sequencers, L2-M4's directions, and this module's four shapes of place. Fourteen words in S10 and the only new thing in the module is the name of a city — which is what a ninth module of a fourth level should feel like.

words.note: 'When' with a subjunctive — M6's reading. A case after cum means 'with'.
'At Rome' — the LOCATIVE, a surviving case with a handful of members. It is also identical to the genitive, and nothing but the sentence parts them.
'When I was' — the imperfect subjunctive of sum, which cum requires. M3 opened it and M6 used it.
'Every day'. L1-M4's word.
'To', with the object shape after it — required for an ordinary noun.
'Office' after ad. L3-M8's word.
'I used to go' — the imperfect of eō. M8's tense on the shortest verb in the course: eō, ībam, īvī.

sentences.trap: Three of the level's arrivals in one sentence: M6's cum with a mood, M8's imperfect, and this module's locative. None of them is new by itself and the combination is what a ninth module of a fourth level should be able to build.

words.note: 'From Rome' — the ablative, with no preposition. Rōmam goes to, Rōmā comes from, Rōmae is at.
'Straight on' — L2-M4's ablative doing an adverb's job: 'by a straight route'. No preposition, like the city.
'Home' — the to-shape, with no preposition.

'To', with the object shape after it.

sentences.trap: Four things in the ablative or accusative and only one preposition among them. Rōmā, rēctā and domum each carry their own relation, and ad dextram does not — which is the whole of this module beside L2-M4's directions, and the count of prepositions in a Latin journey is far lower than in an English one.
